Icoana este pictată pe un suport de lemn de formă dreptunghiulară, avînd o ramă profilată. Iisus -Învățător sau Hristos Ușa, redatbust. Părul lung, căzînd pe umeri, mustață și barbă scurtă, despicată în două, ochii mari, plini de pace, În jurul capului are nimbul cruciger, trasat cu linii albe, subțiri.Pe cap poartă coroană de "Împărat al Cerului și al Pământului", împodobită cu pietre scumpe și perle. Cu mâna dreaptă binecuvintează, în stânga ține cartea Sfintelor Evanghelii deschisă, cu textul amintit. Tunica este de culoare verde închis, cămașa roșie, mijocul încins cu un brîu subțire, negru. Arhetipul acestei icoane este foarte vechi. Trăsăturile ei esențiale se disting într-o frescă realizată în sec. al IV lea pe tavanul Catacombei lui Commodilla din Roma. Fondul icoanei este întunecat, rama neagră prezintă 4 șănțulețe puțin adânci,realizate prin scobire. Dosul icoanei este tăiat special pentru a se îmbina cu rama. Este prevăzută cu două pene în relief și o pană longitudinală.

Houses in the plot of Boikwatho Captain, a San woman living in Sanyedi ward. The house to the left, where her cousin lives, is falling down. The middle house is where his niece stays, and the one on the right where her husband's niece lives. The layout of the plot is unlike others in Sanyedi, with houses facing out to a path rather than into a central living space. Boikwatho explained that this was how her family built in Sehitwa, in a line facing the same direction. She claimed that this was a San tradition, but is more likely to have been a result of Mbanderu influence in Sehitwa.

A view of the sparsely grassed savannah with trees and shrubs beyond, possibly near Pochala. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during March-May this image shows the savannah at the beginning of the rainy season.

Two carriers with baggage on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. The man on the left is Oyo, Evans-Pritchard's Anuak servant and occasional translater. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.

A large and sacred Tamarind tree, located to the west of Pochala near some falls on the Akobo river. This sacred tree was known as "Aboori" after a woman who was buried (wrapped in mats and thornwood) in its branches.

A large and sacred Tamarind tree (with a ?Sycamore to the right), located to the west of Pochala near some falls on the Akobo river. This sacred tree was known as "Aboori" after a woman who was buried (wrapped in mats and thornwood) in its branches.

A group of carriers in the distance resting during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935. This sort of grassy plain is characteristic of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo, and may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935.

Two forked posts and a carved fence support (dikweri) indicate that this entrance way to a homestead is that of one of the nobles of Ukaadi, possibly the leading noble Akwei-war-Alal. Near the entrance is a tree with a thick trunk, probably a shaded seating area known as wic mac. In western and other Anuak districts, such symbols as dikweri adorn the compound of a headman.

Zagbeli. Bound comb made by lashing palm ribs together with palm leaf fibre. Two types of binding made of palm leaf fibre; one has probably failed (the twisted vertical fibres) and another was put in place (the flat kind of binding).
Kiyaga. A shallow, square twilled basketry tray of natural colour, for winnowing grain. The rim is reinforced with two strips of cane, and each corner is reinforced with strips of fibre.
Rat trap. Cylindrical trap of multi-directional plaited cane, tapering slightly toward a bound plant fibre handle. Inside the trap are four wooden sticks with thorns attached to the inner surface.
Kpakpali. Straw hat of natural and dark brown plant fibres, narrow brim with deep(it) crown, pair of stiffeners at crown fixed into a X position.
A group of men and boys at a dance. The men are wearing barkcloth loincloths (bagadi), straw hats and are carrying sticks.

A man at the home of Bambatu seated on a stool wearing a straw hat and barkcloth loincloth, tending an earthenware cooking pot on a small fire containing Bingiya (Bingia) medicine. This medicine was one of the most important of hunting medicines, although it was believed to have other effects also. Bambatu is the man to the right.

A tuka or spirit shrine, consisting of a forked tree trunk or branch, with a bowl containing offerings set in the fork. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead. This shrine has numerous medicines growing around it, including sarawa, ranga ambiri and giango (cactus plant).

Women with large open-weave baskets (type known as bangiribambamba - eye-shaped weave) that are to be filled with beaten eleusine. This crop was once the most important base for porridge and beer, but has been displaced to some extent by manioc, a highly drought and pest resistent tuber, which is however somewhat less nutrious than flour produced from grain such as eleusine.
A group of three men, two wearing barkcloth and one in shirt and waistcoat (half shaved head).  One of the men is identified as wiri Ondosi, i.e. a son of Ondosi.

Women preparing to put bundles of eleusine coracana (millet) grain into large openwork baskets (type known as bangiribambamba, with eye-shaped open weave), ready for immersing in a nearby pool. Once dampened, the grain is laid out in the sun to germinate, an intial stage in the brewing of millet beer, gbangara.

A trough zither, with a hollow body and a curved base, ornamented at each end with concave cut-outs at the corners and incised grooves. There is a conical, rod-like handle at one end. The zither is strung with a single string made from fibre; it is strung across the body of the zither six times through holes at both ends of the trough. The string has come undone at one end. There are three sets of sheet iron squares attached the bottom of the body of the zither, to act as jingles. According to the collector, it would have been held in both hands and played with the thumbs.

A drinking cup made from a coconut shell with an ornate geometric design of bands and squares carved into the outside. It has a long, cylindrical wooden handle with carved decoration, that goes through a hole in the side of the cup. Pyrography has been used to decorate these carved sections.

Huts in the compound of Kesego Ntema and her sisters in Morutseng, using lethlaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) for walling and fencing. The thatched rectilinear hut to right is where their grandmother sleeps, with a thatched kitchen and windscreen close by.
Boitlhoko Garebakwena (left) and a relative collecting morogo wa thepe plant growing in the areas around Matlapaneng ward in the rainy season. The leaves are cooked liked spinach.

Portrait of Kefilwe Hadisa in her plot in Sanyedi ward, outside a hut used to accommodate visiting relatives. Kefilwe is the niece of Koi Kadisa, who gave her this piece of land to build on some years after she came to Maun to go to school, from where she was born in Boyei.

View of the exterior of the surrounding lolwapa courtyard fence made from letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis), at the home of Naroxoh Mayezi, a Yeyi woman living in Mabadutsa ward. A shade shelter is just visible to left.

A partially ruined house made from mud brick and drinks cans, in the home of Ditshupelo Sanyame, a Yeyi man living in Sankuyo village. This combination of walling in rectilinear form is inherently weak and susceptible to collapse following heavy rains.

A cooking shelter with a windbreak incorporating drinks cans and concrete plaster, in the plot of Keokeditswe Sarefo, a Yeyi woman living in Matumo ward. Sometimes people used wet concrete like this, in a similar manner to mud, without realising that the concrete would burn their skin. A number of people told me that they had burned their hands in this manner.

Kesego Kgalalo (in yellow shawl) with her children and grandchildren. Kesego was the mother of Morton's fieldwork assistant Boitlhoko. The girl in the pink dress is Bonana. The son standing behind Kesego is Lekgoana, and the son standing second from right is Dombas. Her daughter Botšale is holding her new baby Gaorethoa.

The homestead of Tsele Mothowamorena (born 1914), a Yeyi man living in the Gweghiri molapo area near Shorobe village. The homestead includes huts for his cousin in foreground (daughter of his paternal uncle) and nephew in far distance.
Portrait of Dash Maphomo outside his house in Gabamutsha, a molapo farming area west of Shorobe.
A circular hut with walling made from drinks cans collected from a local bar (ntlo ya ditini). In the homestead of Mpepi Morapedi, a Yeyi woman from Shorobe now living in Wenela Ward.

A three-quarter length portrait of four men (identified as three Gumuz men and one Shilluk - probably to the right) wearing arabic-style white tunics. Evans-Pritchard notes that he met a small colony of Gumuz people, who had come from western Ethiopia in small groups over the years, around Roseires. They were (and are) predominantly muslim and besides agriculture kept small numbers of cattle and other livestock.

Seven men and youths sat on the ground outside a building made of wooden poles and mud with a thatched roof. The youth second from the left is playing a geedal, or bow harp, a seven-stringed musical instrument, and is using both hands to pluck the strings. The instrument consists of a sound box, in one end of which is inserted a curved stick that projects outwards and upwards. On this stick are attached seven tuning pegs. A string is strung from each peg and attached to the sound box. The youth second from the right is sitting on a carved  upturned vessel that is goblet shaped.

None of the people named here are still alive [NJL 02/04/2012]

Mowanja building a mondumé (harp zither), a musical instrument. The man holds one end of a long stick in his mouth and a string is stretched the length of the stick and passes through a notch of a wooden bridge that is wedged in the stick  and raises the string above the stick. The man appears to be about the fix another string in place. Some wood shavings and a large blade lie on the ground in the foreground. Behind the man three people and a child are sitting outside a dome-shaped shelter.

A small stone enclosure used as a men's squatting place, visited by the Seligmans in the early part of 1922. According to their diary they travelled between these Lotuko villages by bicycle. The Seligman's noted that although common among the Lokoiya, such meeting enclosures were not found among the Tarangole territorial group of Lotuko. Labalwa, although a Lotuko settlement, was not part of this group.

A youth places his hand on the shoulder of a girl standing in a raised position beside him, a pipe in her mouth and temples shaved. She is wearing a number of beads, probably given to her by male admirers such as this youth.

A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari girls wearing textile waist cloths and strings of beads around their necks [blurred image], other children gathered near them at the edge of the frame. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women.

A three-quarter length portrait of two young Mandari women in a cattle camp wearing textile waist cloths and a large number of mostly red bead strings around their waist, as well as some around the neck [poor negative]. Such bead strings were often given to young women by courting male youths. Youths wear such rem beads as a way of denoting their age grade grouping and for display.
A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari women wearing textile body cloths, strings of beads, and metal arm ornaments.

A three-quarter length portrait of a Mandari woman leaning against the thatch of a hut, wearing metal arm ornaments and a short fringed apron. She has several bands of vertical cicatrice dots on her abdomen.

A formal portrait of a seated man in a military uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955), possibly ranking as a sargeant, with five women and two children posing around him, all wearing Mandari ornaments and clothing. Behind them is a large rectilinear thatched building, probably a communal building for soldiers and their dependants. These women may be wives or family members of the soldier living with him at the military post.

View of a Datooga boy sat inside a hut 20 miles west of Katesh, Tanzania. The boy is grasping at the robes of a person standing up, and is surrounded by items of daily life such as pots, baskets, wooden stools and two grinding stones with ground flour. A kid goat is taking an interest in the flour on one of the stones.

Portrait of a Datooga woman sat inside a hut next to two hanging gourd pots in a settlement 20 miles west of Katesh, Tanzania. She is wearing gold and ivory bracelets on her arm, and around her neck is a wide coiled gold collar and a variety of multicoloured bead necklaces. Her ear lobes are stretched with a gold ornamental earring and her eyes are ringed with scarification marks.

According to its original caption, this photograph was taken in connection with a ruined Luo stonewalled settlement of a type known as ohinga to archaeologists of the region, possibly at Kanyipir village. Such ruins are common in Luo country, particularly in South Nyanza District. Many of these settlements date to the nineteenth century and some may be contemporary with the earthwork settlements known as gunda bur, elsewhere photographed by Evans-Pritchard. The three men posing for the camera are unidentified, but they all appear to be in the employ of the colonial administration due to their clothing. The one on the left is wearing a chief's helmet (simba) and may be the man called Okoth identified in 1998.349.213. The man in the middle appears in 1998.349.215 while the other two appear in 1998.349.213. [Gilbert Oteyo & CM 11/04/2007]

A family group posed in front of a homestead, with a woman and girl standing behind a man wearing a skin seated in profile on a low stool. They are all wearing metal arm and ankle ornaments as well as strings of beads. The image seems to have been taken sometime in January 1879 when Buchta travelled through Acholi country en route to Bunyoro.

A view across an Acholi homestead, with a grave-shrine or kac visible to the left, in front of the entrance to a hut. The kac consists of a four-corned rack to a height of three or four feet, with a 'four-peg shrine' near one corner, including a notched stake. The spirit of the deceased (tipo) is regarded as existing in the earth below the kac, and makes itself heard in dreams. This particular kac was said to be that of a rain-maker's father (possibly called Akona of Falonganji clan), in a village in the hill country immediately south of Lotuko country, probably Magwe.

An upper body full face portrait of an Acholi man, also photographed by Buchta as an 'Acholi warrior' in another image. He is wearing metal arm and neck rings as well as a leopard skin around his shoulders. His hair is ornamented by stringwork and a plume at the back of his head. The image seems to have been taken sometime in January 1879 when Buchta travelled through Acholi country en route to Bunyoro.

A wooden stirrer for stirring porridge, BARI. It is placed on the ground for photographing. Porridge is the non-fermented form, which, when fermented becomes 'beer'. Porridge can be made from ground sorghum (durrha), sesame (simsim) and groundnuts. Sorghum alone is quite sour, sesame sweetens it. A light porridge Deborah compared with tea - "it warms your blood." Porridge has a smooth consistency, and can be thick or quite liquid. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

A young girl sits on the ground, weaving  basket. The fronds (DIRI) are made from the  DURA plant. The basket-maker makes a small square basket base as in the image. A set of old stone axe-heads and other stones, laid out on the ground by Surur the rain-maker for Evans-Pritchard to photograph them (although not touch them) from their home in a pot beneath the eaves of his hut, which also contained some of his hair clippings. These stones were called landa loma - stones of Loma, a spiritual connection with rain-making. During rain-making Surur would place these stones along with magical medicines in a pot with rock-pool water and sprinkle to the east where the next day was to arrive from.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) stuck into the ground under a large tree with a shorter notched post (lingi) for hunting-magic offerings, usually fowl sacrifice. During drought the rain-post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

Two carved wooden funerary figures, one with large horns set on top of a low earth burial mound within a homestead. Not all Bongo graves were marked with a mound of stones, and such mounds were sometimes erected a number of years later at a mortuary ceremony. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose. Usually accompanied by tallies of animals killed in hunting, the horns on the figure signify the status of the hunter.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) with maize heads and medicines attached, stuck into the ground under a large nilotic shea-butter tree, Vitellaria paradoxa ssp. nilotica, a slow-growing hardwood fruit tree indigenous to northern Uganda and Southern Sudan. During drought this post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them); the first a likeness of the deceased, the next clockwise a forked (horn-shaped) post set up by his son-in-law yet tallying his own buffalo kills. The next (only tip visible) is a likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then a forked post tallying six rhino and lastly a forked post tallying five buffalo [cloudy image at centre].

A number of cattle making their way across a plain, with a light coloured ox with tasselled decoration on its upright left horn, its right horn trained backwards. Youth decorated their favourite oxen in this manner for aesthetically pleasing effects, and the identification between them and their ox was such that they took their initiated name and prestige from it. In contrast to his two earlier fieldwork visits when photographing cattle was viewed suspiciously by the Nuer, Evans-Pritchard took numerous record images of them during his later field trips.
A dark image of a youth with hands raised to his face, standing next to a large woodfuel pile for steamers on the Sobat River.

A distant view of a cluster of huts comprising a cattle camp, seen across a wide expanse of treeless grass savannah in western Nuerland. Dry season camps in western Nuerland were often formed close to pools and other more permanent water sources, whereas in eastern Nuerland large rivers such as the Sobat and Nyanding were favoured.
Looking towards a camp in Western Nuerland, with numerous cattle tethered amongst small huts. The hut in the foreground has mud-plastered walls and a small thatched top twisted into a finial.

A clay ox as made by Nuer children, complete with large hump and ash markings, placed on a stool with a woven grass perimeter fence as a backdrop. In other images it is clear that this was a courtyard fence at a mission or government property, most likely at Nasir.
The hut and cattle byre (luak) roofs of a homestead can just be seen against the skyline [poor photo].

A view across the cleared area of a village homestead (gol) with cattle lying down in the middle ground and a cattle byre (luak) to the left, a sleeping hut to the right and the cattle byre (luak) of another homestead beyond. In the central cleared area can just be seen a firescreen (buor) against which a cooking-fire is made. Often these firescreens incorporated three humps on the top, and were a symbol of a woman's status as a wife and mother of a household. Sacrifices were often made near to the buor of the homestead.

The canvas tent used by Evans-Pritchard during his Nuer fieldwork placed under a tree for shade. A chair sits in the doorway with boxes of various provisions stored under the tent-flaps. The location is probably at a village site, possibly in the Bahr-el-Ghazal region, and therefore possibly during Evans-Pritchard's first field trip in 1930.

Edward Ross, with his truck, and Dr. David Spain (a social anthropologist) visiting Kanuri Chief Lawan Mustafa at his home in Konduga Village, 25 miles east of Maiduguri, and two other men. Mustafa is the headman of the village and is wearing an expensive embroidered blue cap and robe. It is the custom to visit the headman first when entering a village.

Shetima, one of the five sons of the chief of Konduga Village, riding through the village on horseback. The horse is wearing ornate horse gear. The bridle has a red, white and blue cloth browband and a leather noseband both with a number of black and red tassles dangling from it, and embossed white metal cheeckpieces with tassels. The saddle features similar ornamental designs, including a white metal breastcollar with blue, red and white cloth drape. A sheepskin hide is draped over the horse's back. Shetima is wearing a blue flowing robe and a red cap.

Anderson Willy with his wife and daughter outside their home in Boseja Ward, Maun. Anderson moved to Maun from the Mbukushu settlement of Etsha in 1982.

A hut in the plot of Jobe Phezo, a woman living in Boseja ward, showing the preferred Mbukushu method of building, using a meshwork of mopane poles between uprights and packing the gaps with wet soil to dry into place. Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River. This hut belonged to the son of one of Jobe's aunts (her cousin).

A house in the plot belonging to the younger brother of Wambe Angere, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born at Sepupa, where her parents were still living. The hut is made from mopane poles lashed together in a meshwork and plastered in between with soil from termite mounds (mmu wa seolo). The structure for another building can be seen to left.
A cylindrical basket. This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.

Hut belonging to the eldest son of Kashiate Mogumbula, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born in Angola who moved with her parents to Etsha 3, gradually moving to Maun and this ward. She stated that she only found people building like this, using dithupa (a meshwork of sticks) packed with earth, here in Boseja. It seemed to her to be a very localised style in this ward due to difficulties of accessing mud bricks or money for concrete bricks, or money for letlhaka.
Matomo James, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward, constructing a lolwapa courtyard fence in front of his house using stems of mokodi (wild sage) and lebelebele (millet) from his garden.
A lidded basket in the form of a three-legged cooking pot (potjie in Afrikaans). This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.
The homestead of Moffat Mokhawa in Matlapaneng ward, showing his planting of shrubs and fruit trees around the plot.

Two men wearing dammur cloth, photographed by Evans-Pritchard during his brief two day visit to the hill, the peoples of which speak a dialect of Burun. He also noted however that some people identified themselves as an exogenous group known as Fuin, who formed an aristocratic group with a 'king' who was frequently in danger of regicide from other potential leaders. But this group seems mostly to have been absorbed by Burun.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the east side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela A, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument faces south and stands in line with the stelae C and D in front of the mound which forms the northern boundary of the Great Plaza. Owing to the decayed condition of the stone, the design on the pedestal which supports the figure is somewhat obscure both on the front and on the back of the monument; but in each case parts of the profile of a grotesque mask can be traced.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 1) to 9.17.5.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 775 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the east side of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph G, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument is lying on a foundation of three flat stone slabs. For want of a better name my companions in camp were accustomed to call this monument "the armadillo". The arms and legs of the animal portrayed are in much the same position as those on the dragon B, but there are no scrolls on the elbows and knees such as are always found on the dragons. The wrists and ankles are adorned with bracelets and anklets, and the skin is plated with flattened disks or scales.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 7) to 9.17.15.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 785 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years as various different animals, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a 'Waterlily Jaguar', with human figures emerging from both ends. The monument was created during the first year of the reign of Sky Xul and records details of the funeral ceremony of his predecessor K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the west side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela K, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument faces nearly east and west. When first found in 1883 about three feet of the sculpture was buried in the ground. There is no carved pedestal. From the squat shape of the human figure it was always known to us as "The Dwarf". [...] The feather canopy on the west face is father more prominent than usual. On the east face the ornament is somewhat damaged and weather-worn. The human face is very well preserved, and is remarkable for the full and rounded features.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 11) to 9.19.0.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 805 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the reign of Jade Sky. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a Hopi man, sitting on the ground in front of a vertical loom, weaving a sacred blanket.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[t]his class of weaving is done exclusively by the men and the work of preparing sacred blankets is always conducted in an estufa.  The [Hopi] sacred blanket is quite different from that made by the Navajoes.  The body of it is always white with the borders embroidered.'

View of multi-storeyed buildings at Oraibi pueblo on Third Mesa, with crops drying on a roof in the foreground.  According to an original note by James Stevenson (prepared circa 1885), Oraibi 'occupies a position on the top of a mesa on the opposite side of a broad valley some twelve miles west of [Shongopavi]. [...] These people are situated so remotely from the ordinary routes of travel that they are less frequently visited by white people. [...] Their village is old and in bad repair; their people are the best known of all the pueblos and comprise a population of about 700, which equals all the other [Hopi] pueblos combined.'

View (looking southward from Tewa pueblo) of Sichomovi pueblo (in the middle distance) and Walpi pueblo (in the far distance).  These Hopi settlements, built on First Mesa, appear to run together but are in fact separate and distinct, with the interior court of Tewa (and crops drying on a roof) prominent in the foreground.  According to an original note by James Stevenson (prepared circa 1885), the 'mesa is about 700 feet above the surrounding plain, and is only reached by narrow pathways, only one of which is passable for horses and burros.  The mesa is composed of solid sandstone and its summit embraces an area of about one-half mile, narrowing as it extends to the location of W[a]lpi.  Between W[a]lpi and the other two villages [Tewa and Sichomovi] the mesa diminishes to a width of ten feet over which all communication with W[a]lpi must be had.  The constant travel over this mesa has worn paths to the depth of several inches in the solid rock.'

Pinya. Fishing harpoon or spear with barbed point. Long wooden shaft with circular cross-section tapering towards the butt; shaft also tapers slightly towards the top which is socketed; narrow point with a single barb, fixed in place with cord and resin; band of black resin around the shaft near the point and on the butt.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural geometric pattern with four central rows of monkey motifs within squares, and a row of lizards at the top and bottom.
Cleft piece of barberry wood, an implement used for detaching limpets from rocks.
Woven bag with woven handle. Simple loop or button-hole stritch. Used for carrying cartridges etc. Made with Chambria. Bought for eight cartridges ie. three days work. Carried by men only.
Long necklace of very small trade beads. Bead colour include blue, yellow, and white. Made and worn by women.
Espingo chain made of seeds or nuts in shells. Medicine used for stomach ache, collected by Aguaruna. Five seeds detached but present.

Chikai. Beaded dance girdle or belt. Design of white truncated lozenges with central black cross on a black and blue background with white border. Glass beads are strung on twisted vegetable fibres between two lengths of cotton-wrapped cane and reinforced with vertical fibres at intervals; cotton ties extend from both canes, presumably used for fastening. Two loose strings of beads and a bag of black and white beads.
Goabddá. Divination drum with designs on the skin membrane and openwork carving on the base.

Wooden double cup, carved with a four-headed snake design. A handle with incised rhombs in the snake’s body connects the two cups. A projection at each side of the cups is carved with snake’s heads. The shape of the cups can be described as quadrangular, while the four sides are almost bent in a sickle shape and the four corners are flattened.
Ladle - A wooden carved ladle with incisions of human figures on the bowl. The handle shows three human figures, one of them is encased by a snake up to the shoulder and another one is crouching.

Black velvet, crescent-shaped woman’s collar, backed with floral patterned cloth. Front decorated at centre and either side with anthropomorphic faces wearing ovoid linear headdresses, intersected by butterflies and snakes in yellow, orange, green and white glass beads. Sequins and small bead crosses with sequins at centre dispersed between main figures. Bands at top and bottom of repeated groups of beads arranged in triangles. Lower edge stitched with sequins and aluminium chain, which is strung with aluminium plaques, decorated with leaves and flowers, spade-shaped ornaments and small metal bells. Four cowrie shells stitched on front centre and sides. Press studs along one top edge with short cream fabric ties on top interior edge.

Teapot of 'ribbed' design. The body reproduces the shape of a pumpkin, the handle a piece of the stalk, and the spout a leaf. Stamps giving the name of the maker on the base, under the lid (twice) and under the handle. The pot and lid are made of dark red-brown pottery with pale flecks.

The teapot, 2004.183 A-B was packed for transport inside a red and black paper covered cardboard box, not original to the pot. Inside the box, the teapot is supported by a polystyrene stand covered with a bright yellow synthetic silk fabric. The front of the box has been damaged by the removal of adhesive tape.

S'us'utr. Beaded headdress made by Gul Sahar. Made from a piece of woven black woollen fabric and heavily embellished with panels of yellow, green and black beads, and white buttons and small metal bells. Part of a Kalasha costume.
One of ten paintings of Manipuri tribesmen of Assam, painted by a Manipuri artist. Kuki man. Forms a pair with 1951.764.10.

Urgyan (Urgyani Phahibo Ngha). Headdress formed of five upright sections of painted paper, each with a representation of an ancestor, held together with cloth band which is tied at the back of the head when worn.
Bakhu. Traditional cape made of hand-woven sheep's wool. Worn mainly by men, but in the past women would also wear them.
Ra thih. Bag. Goat skin with string, rolled and used as a container for sacred material.
Chyha (Neme). Soul catcher staff, used by Khhlyaprin shaman.
Sword; Sheath; Knife - " Old sword from the dead house" (according to label). A: short, leaf- shaped knife, with sheath. B: bilaterally tanged " sword"

Metal necklace with multiple pendants on chains. Penannular twited torc necklace with hook and eye fitting set with an oval red stone; eleven circular loops welded onto the torc supporting a decorative fringe with pendants; six long lengths of chain each with a subrectangular metal plate, a hollow sphere and semi-circular plate alternating with five shorter lengths of chain with teardrop-shaped pendant; metal pendants are set with blue and red glass beads.

Metal hair ornament consisting of a string of beads with coin fringe. String of hollow spherical beads alternating with hollow drop-shaped filigree pendants with two coins hanging from each; strung on a length of cord.
Bös. A dark red silk sash with a pattern in the weft at regular intervals.

Cloak made from yak skin, cotton and wool with attached disc ornaments and tassels. Yak skin with brown hair, skin side facing out; along the top is a rectangular length of black felted wool backed with blue cotton cloth and bordered at the top with a strip of black velvet; two large and seven small disc ornaments made from three layers wrapped in green, pink and blue cotton and embroidered on the top with concentric motifs of lines and triangles in white, red, blue, pink, orange, black, green and blue; the two large discs have stylised birds at the centre, the small discs have two long tassels of leather hanging from the middle; two cream cotton ties embroidered with black geometric motifs at the pointed ends.

Long blouse of blue cotton. Long, wide sleeves, round collar and long body, with side slits on the front sides and is longer at the back. It closes on the right seam using an overlapping panel and four knot and loop fastenings; it closes below the neck using two gold coloured metal buttons, which depict a bird and fruit with leaves engraved on the obverse. The collar, panel and side slits have a very dark blue trim, with a black and white woven trim on the panel and at the left side slit.
Spear head. Made of iron, leaf-shaped, and tanged at the end.
Bracelet, small and penannular in shape. Made from a bent brass rod, with a small opening at the end of the two pieces. Some incision marks at one of the ends of the rod. Worn by Vedda peoples.
A rectangular piece of brown bark, lightly engraved with a drawing of a stick carrying two jars at either end, used as a demand for honey.
Necklace (in tin); a letter describing acquisition is included.
Hat or helmet of oval form with domed crown and narrow brim. Made of closely plaited cane strengthened with thick cane strips.; Good; Whole.

Woman's sleeveless jacket in cream and blue with embroidery on the back. Made from two panels of cream or undyed cotton with a wide blue border joined at the back; sewn together at the back and the side with the arm holes and front open; decorated at the back with geometric designs in red, yellow, blue and white; hem at the front is decorated with red and blue thread.

Blow pipe quiver; bamboo, decorated with patterns (probably charms), with pandanus leaf cap and rattan binding; carrying string is of wild bread fruit bark. Individual small bamboo tubes within, to hold pith butted darts for a wooden blow pipe; these tubes are fastened together in a strip, and then wound up to fit the quiver; they can be drawn out by pulling the inner string
Axe  - Axe head. Worn over shoulder by ordinary tribesmen.

Ãepiec. Woman's cap. The body of the cap has embroidered motifs in white, red, yellow, green, pink, and blue. The top of the cap is made of a lilac fabric with embroidered decorations, and a woven panel is sewn to the bottom.
Woman's apron. The fabric is blue with a white dot pattern, and is tightly pleated. A strip of red fabric with a floral pattern is sewn to the top to form part of the strings.
A piece of cloth with embroidered patterns in red, blue, yellow, green, purple, pink, and blue. Possibly a piece of an unfinished cap.
A strip of fur, roughly rectangular in shape. The fur is brown, cream and grey, and the skin has puncture- marks along one of the longer edges, indicating that it was once sewn to something.
Pin made of blackthorn wood, untrimmed, made by Leviathon Pickett. One terminal tapers to a point, the other has an extending, right angled protrusion. Natural knots present on the wood.

Tamata. Votive offering. Stylised representation of an eye, hand modelled in green wax to form a flat, oval shape. A black-eyed bean has been pushed into the centre of one side and is surrounded by several radiating grooves. There is a large loop of string attached to the top suggesting a point of suspension.
Tamata. Votive offering of a baby's face and neck made from cast and sheet silver, soldered together. Hole at the top of head for the attachment of a safety pin.

Bilum, almost square bag netted from thick twine in double figure of 8 rows. Natural and reddish brown loop stitching attaches separately netted rim band. Netted carrying strap crosses over from top corners. Design in contrasting blue and reddish brown dyed twine against natural pale brown colour. At top a complex zigzag of striped trapezoids with chequered parallelograms, partly linked across top by border band of brown, and joined across bottom by series of blue, brown and blue narrow bands. In centre a thick brown stripe with ribbed top, then four narrow ribbed bands, brown, blue, brown, blue. Below a large complex zigzag with large parallelograms spacing out the trapezoids. Made by Tshuosh, in neighbourhood of Berui village. Some stains. Original accession notes: " Pattern worked in dyed string. Carried suspended from the head by women. Bought from Tshuosh by Iatmul." Fair.

Human head on tiered trunk with a bird each side of trunk centre, and 2-pronged hook base. Elaborate facial paint on head, cowrie shell eye inlay, grooved forehead. With fibre tassels. Attributed by Iatmul to Tshambuli.

Beater for gong. Stick with expanded base, cylindrical handle and carved tapering point, with janus heads at bottom. Tip broken off. Lugs at right angles to faces rather than same sides as in 1930.576. Separated by tiny triangular knobs. Heads have oval raised eyes (one head with ring carved inside the ovals), delicate club noses and raised crescent mouths.

Lens-shaped light wood head with red/brown paint overall and rounded back. Small rounded head cap, sharply raised slant eyes. Bulbous nose with narrow flanges for nostrils. Down-curved mouth. Laterally pierced ' bearded' chin. No ears.

Ovoid pith head attached to centre of buttock ornament 1935.8. A few coils of hair remain on top of head and many empty holes for more coils. Face painted with fine black lines against dark yellow background.

Bow-legged wooden figure, painted on its front only. Round face with triangular nose, rough pit eyes and raised crescent lips, tiny pierced semioval ear lugs. Black knob nipples and white knob knee cap. Painted mainly red with touches of black and white. White raised pubic area with vulva slit painted in red, narrow belly with white ring round black navel. White crescent pendant/necklace, and white curves from nipples across chest. Black cap on head, black surround to eyes and as a median line on the nose. Red raised mouth with red and white stripes across the remainder of the face. Raised triangular lug on the back of the head with a fibre strand looped through it for hanging up. In this box is a fibre belt (?) probably broken off one of the figures (1935.146 or 1935.147). Original accession notes: " Wooden female figure, coloured red and marked with white patterns. There is a lug behind the head for suspension. It was probably carved for amusement, but is possibly totemic - the one theory does not exclude the other. Totemism is not always a very serious matter." Good

Arrow with three blackened wooden points bound together near base with cane. One point has only widely spaced, small alternate side barbs, other two have additional nicks along the ridges between the side barbs. No foreshaft. Shaft binding of diagonally crossed fine cane or other fibre? Tapering bamboo shaft with remains of red stain.

Pam au. A rounded necked sago earthenware jar. Applique face on one side of neck only. Pointed slightly hooked nose, double oval ring eyes and oval ring chain below similar double oval ring mouth. Plan fibre tassels through double pierced ear arcs in line with beak.

Circular wooden stool with concave seat resting on two slab legs which have been reconstructed. Low relief sinuous designs on outward facing face of legs. The seat is decorated with open work sinuous designs including inset cowrie shells and copper alloy tacks. The legs are slotted into the seat and attached with groups of copper alloy nails.
Large two-handled pot with sharp carination. Internally glazed and decorated with bands of dark glaze and pink ornament: Dar, Thebana and Jerida (the horse, the fly and the palm leaf.
A necklace made of polished seeds; spherical black interspersed with 22 biconical red Abrus precatorius seeds.
Large pot of burnished black ware. Everted rim, narrow and tall neck, globular body and rounded base. Decorated with horizontal line at base of neck. Sections of rim broken away and missing.
Pottery vessel, of light red clay, with an everted circular rim, long neck, bulbous body, circular foot and an open base. Light circular grooves visible above the shoulder.

Pot of burnished red ware. Everted rim with small mouth and very narrow neck, rounded body with flat base. Decorated above shoulder and below neck with linear markings incised with a stick. Three horizontal lines with filled triangles and vertical rows of short lines.

Pair of ridged circular armlets. Black leather with white leather sewn through the centre with brown leather strips plaited to connect the two ends of the armlets. (A) is missing areas of leather. (B) is bent out of shape. Bought in Sebilla market, Kusasi tribe.

A rectangular cloth made from multiple panels of cream cotton sewn together. There are wide grey and red woven stripes, and embroidery in dark blue, including double vertical stripes of small square stitches along the top, and bands of geometric pattern and zig-zags. A rectangular section has been cut from one edge.
Crook or staff made from dark wood.
A rectangular piece of white cotton possibly used as a breast band or a waist band, previously described as a cummerbund. The cotton has possibly been starched.

A necklace consisting of small faceted gold gilt beads strung and dangling ovoid shaped gold gilt beads, strung onto a length of plant fibre. It is fastened by a loop of plant fibre and a gold gilt bead at the ends.

Necklace with golden pointed ovoid pendants. 14 filled pendants with a horizontal pointed ovoid form hanging from two loops; pendants alternate with groups of seven or eight faceted brass beads with a gilded surface; fastened with a loop of cord and a faceted bead. Strung on cotton cord.
One of ten paintings of Manipuri tribesmen of Assam, painted by a Manipuri artist. Meiti woman. Forms a pair with 1951.764.1.
Necklace comprising string of imitation coral beads strung on red thread. Worn by young men and women.
Arrow  - Four bamboo arrows, with sharpened ends butt no separate heads. Triple straight feathering.
Fragment from the shaft of an arrow. Wood with circular cross-section, wrapped with black fibre. Broken at both ends and damaged by insects.

Simple bow with possible recurve. Wooden bow with circular cross-section tapering towards either end; leather strip at one end to prevent string from slipping. Lighter area of wood indicating missing leather strip.

Tsipune. A man's long sleeveless coat made from black wool, with a pleated back. The front is open and trimmed with a brown braiding, with a wide decorative area of brown braiding at the chest; the arm holes, chest pocket and two side pockets are also trimmed with brown braiding.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in cream wool with pink toes. For festive wear. Tied together.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of blue, black, brown, orange, purple and pink. Tied together.

Tsipune. A man's long sleeveless coat made from black wool, with a heavily pleated back. The front is open and trimmed with a brown braiding, with a wide decorative area of brown braiding at the chest; the arm holes, chest pocket and two side pockets are also trimmed with brown braiding. The pleats are stitched together with unspun wool.

A pair of red, black and white garters woven into long rectangular bands with loops and one end, and long plaited ties with tassels ends at the other. Woven with a background and a central row of red, with white triangles along either side.
A pair of men’s white linen drawers, with short legs and a draw string waistband. Small area of red stitching on the waistband.

A pair of red, black and white garters woven into long rectangular bands with loops and one end, and long plaited ties with tassels ends at the other. Woven with a central row of red and black chevrons, with white triangles along either side and red along the edges.

String of blue glass cylindrical beads with one red bead, worn round the waist. Given to donor by Ikang the rainmaker - woman, then acting with her brother in law - she was the real chief at Tarangole. Possibly used as currency.
Spear. Leaf-shaped, socketed iron head with mid-rib and narrow shank. Tapering wooden shaft.
Tortoise shell cowbell, suspended upon a plaited hide ring and a further attached metal ring.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; translucent red and opaque white beads.

Spoon made of horn for porridge matama and mwele. The spoon has a large bowl, and short handle with a circular cross-section. There is a perforation at the end of the hole, with a loop of hide or sinew tied through. The bowl has a split in it, which has a contemporary repair made with hide or sinew stitches.

Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped with a prominent midrib; long split socket; part of the socket has come away and is missing. The shaft has a circular cross-section, and terminates with a metal ferrule.

Pipe, with a tapering wooden stem and black ceramic bowl. The bowl is conical with convex sides and is decorated with a human face, including an incised mouth, protruding ears and nose, and eyes that have been highlighted with white pigment.

Emomi. A shield made from thick hippopotamus hide with a wooden handle. Roughly circular in shape with a curved cross-section, there are two lobes and a folded edge. The reverse has a centred wooden handle across the diameter, that has been bound and secured in place with strips of brown and black leather. Decorated with scored, tightly intersecting lines.
An ivory armlet with a rectangular cross section of vary thickness. Interior dark red colour, exterior light orange colour.

Raft-rattle made from thin lengths of bamboo lashed together with plant fibre to create a hollow rectangular rattle. The ends are sealed, one with beige cloth, the other with blue cloth, both with a cowrie shell. Seeds inside create the rattle sound.
Rattle. Four wooden sticks, each stick has three hollow seed pods containing seeds. They are held together with twine at one end and cloth at the other end.
One stone axe. Tapering towards a narrow flat butt end; slightly straight retouched cutting edge; curved sides, oval cross-section. Smooth surface towards the cutting edge.
